title: Here's How and Why to Use Guided Meditation as a Teacher During COVID 2020
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com), guest post by Camille Napier Bernstein, September 3,
summary: In this guest post, longtime Massachusetts English teacher Camille Napier Bernstein — introduced by Dave Stuart Jr. as a correspondent whose thinking he trusts — explains why she has opened every class with a moment of stillness for over twenty years and why she commissioned a custom guided meditation for teachers to get through the anxiety of pandemic-era teaching. She anticipates the natural skepticism readers might have toward the word 'hypnotherapy,' distinguishing it from brainwashing and citing evidence that hypnosis-based relaxation techniques can reduce stress, improve immune function, and ease PTSD symptoms. Bernstein describes the 13-minute recording made by hypnotherapist Jess Porter, walking through what the meditation does (a body relaxation exercise paired with reminders about the benefits of a relaxed state) and offering practical suggestions for when and where teachers might use it — before bed, first thing in the morning, or even in the school parking lot. The piece is a personal, evidence-referencing case for treating stillness and guided relaxation as a legitimate professional practice for teachers rather than a fringe indulgence.
points: Bernstein frames stillness as a skill she deliberately teaches students over decades, not a one-off trick, noting that former students remember it more than her grammar or thesis-writing instruction.

She proactively addresses the stigma around the word 'hypnotherapy,' distinguishing it from brainwashing and citing research linking hypnosis-based relaxation to reduced stress, improved immune function, and eased PTSD symptoms.
The recommended 13-minute meditation is designed to be usable anywhere — bed, a chair, a picnic blanket, even a car in the school parking lot — lowering the barrier to actually using it.
The practice is framed as instrumentally useful beyond personal relief: a teacher's relaxed state is described as transferring to students, tying self-care directly to classroom climate.
quotes: For over twenty years, I've begun my classes with stillness — first as a crowd-control trick; later, because it's the best skill I know to share with kids.
My former students, years after they've graduated, still contact me to say they heard "Orange Sky," one of the calming songs I use in my class, or thank me for introducing them to meditation.
More than any other year, I have needed meditation to get me through these tough times, and that is why I commissioned a special meditation to speak to our struggle.

I called Jess last week and spoke to the fears teachers have about returning to the classroom and how that anxiety and uncertainty can be paralyzing. Jess got it. But what's more, she found a way to bring that fear — that contracting of heart and mind — under control, expanding it into something beautiful.
Some of you might pause at the word hypnotherapy or hypnosis, assuming it means brainwashing someone into doing silly or harmful things. It's not.
Research has found hypnosis can even alter a person's immune function in ways that offset stress and reduce susceptibility to viral infections.
